summary: Describes version 2 of S/MIME, a way to add cryptographic signatures and encryption to MIME data such as email. It was published as an informational memo, not a standard, and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: S/MIME version 2 adds digital signatures and encryption to MIME data. This RFC defines the message formats and algorithm support expected by its adopters.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email with mime
subtitle: How S/MIME version 2 applies signatures and encryption to MIME entities using PKCS #7.

tldr.problem: MIME data needs mechanisms for authentication, integrity, and privacy when it is sent between systems.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME prepares a canonical MIME entity, processes it into a PKCS #7 object, and wraps that object in MIME. It defines signed and encrypted formats.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2311 is Historic and explicitly says it is historical material, not an IETF standard. It describes RC2/40 as weak encryption.

today: RFC 2311 is Historic and was published as an Informational memo, not an IETF standard. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Security Services for MIME Data
sections.content:
S/MIME adds cryptographic services to MIME data. Digital signatures provide authentication, message integrity, and non-repudiation of origin. Encryption provides privacy and data security.

S/MIME can be used by mail agents or by other systems that carry MIME data, including HTTP transports and automated agents. RFC 2311 states that it is historical material for the public record, not an IETF standard.
sections.plainLanguage: S/MIME can sign MIME data to identify its sender and detect changes. It can also encrypt the data to limit who can read it.

sections.title: Preparing and Wrapping a MIME Entity
sections.content:
The data to be protected is a canonical MIME entity. Before signing or enveloping, the sender prepares the entity, converts its leaf parts to canonical form, and applies a suitable transfer encoding. Text uses CRLF line endings and a named character set.

The sender processes the entity into a PKCS #7 object and wraps that object in MIME. The application/pkcs7-mime type carries one encoded PKCS #7 object. The RFC also defines application/pkcs7-signature for detached signatures and application/pkcs10 for certification requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender prepares the MIME content in a consistent form, then places it inside a PKCS #7 object. A MIME type identifies the kind of protected object being carried.

sections.title: Signed and Encrypted Message Forms
sections.content:
For a clear-signed message, multipart/signed carries the original MIME entity as its first part and a detached signature as its second. A recipient without S/MIME software can still view the first part. The RFC generally prefers this form for sending and says receivers should handle both it and the opaque signedData form.

Signing and enveloping can be nested in either order. Signing first hides the signatories inside the encrypted envelope. Enveloping first leaves the signature available for verification without removing the encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: A clear-signed message keeps readable content beside its detached signature. A sender can also combine signing and encryption by nesting the two formats.

sections.title: Algorithm Support and Selection
sections.content:
Receiving agents must support SHA-1 and MD5 digests and RSA signatures with public keys from 512 to 1024 bits. They must also support decryption with RC2/40 and should support triple DES. Sending agents use recipient capability information when choosing an encryption algorithm.

If recipient capabilities are unknown, the sender may use the algorithm from a previous signed and encrypted message, choose triple DES while accepting a risk of failed decryption, or use RC2/40 when it does not want that risk. A sender that considers weak encryption unacceptable must not use RC2/40.
sections.plainLanguage: Senders can use a recipient's announced capabilities to choose an encryption method. The RFC calls RC2/40 weak and says not to use it when weak encryption is unacceptable.

sections.title: The Risk of Weak Encryption
sections.content:
The RFC says 40-bit encryption offers little actual security over plaintext and is not recommended unless no encryption is the only alternative. A sender should be able to consider the risk before sending with RC2/40 or another weak algorithm.

If the same message is sent once with strong encryption and again with weaker encryption, an observer can decrypt the weaker copy and learn the content of both. The RFC warns against sending a weaker encrypted copy of a message.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC warns that 40-bit encryption offers little protection. If the same content is sent with both strong and weak encryption, the weaker copy can expose it.
